cards.name: Big Five / Five-Factor Model
cards.measures: Five broad trait dimensions — openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism (inverse of emotional stability) — as continuous scores, not categories.
cards.misuse: Reading a score as an identity, or as a prediction of behavior in a specific situation. Traits are tendencies, and situations dominate them.
cards.compatiblePractice: This is the dimensional layer the reflection inventory is aligned with. Bands, not percentiles; retakes over verdicts.

cards.name: HEXACO
cards.measures: Six dimensions — adds Honesty-Humility to a Big Five-like core. Honesty-Humility separates fairness and sincerity from the agreeableness cluster.
cards.misuse: Treating low Honesty-Humility in oneself (or guessing it in someone else) as a character verdict.
cards.compatiblePractice: The inventory's fairness-reciprocity lens is HEXACO-informed: it asks about behavior in specific tempting situations, not about what kind of person you are.

cards.name: Adult attachment (anxiety / avoidance dimensions)
cards.measures: Two independent dimensions — attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance — that vary by relationship and context rather than forming fixed categories.
cards.misuse: The four labels (secure, anxious, avoidant, fearful-avoidant) used as permanent identities. The dimensional research shows within-person variation across relationships.
cards.compatiblePractice: Use the dimension language when reflecting on a specific relationship where pressure appears — 'around this person, approval-seeking gets switched on in me' — never as a label for the other person.

cards.name: Temperament (Rothbart tradition)
cards.measures: Constitutionally based individual differences in reactivity and self-regulation, observable early in development.
cards.misuse: Extending infant/child temperament categories unchanged into adult self-description.
cards.compatiblePractice: Historical context for where trait differences come from; the reflection inventory does not use it directly.

cards.name: MBTI (16 types)
cards.measures: Four binary preferences (E/I, S/N, T/F, J/P) producing 16 type codes. Widely used as a shared vocabulary.
cards.misuse: Treating the code as a validated predictor or a hiring/diagnosis tool. Scores cluster near midpoints and type changes on retest are common.
cards.compatiblePractice: Comparison lens only. The full 16-type guide lives in the Resistance Library (InfoWar ▸ Reading) — read its three rules before the type pages.

cards.name: Enneagram (9 types)
cards.measures: Nine motivation-centered types. The largest systematic review to date (104 samples) found mixed reliability and validity evidence.
cards.misuse: Type assignment as identity or prediction; wing/instinct stacking as diagnostic precision.
cards.compatiblePractice: Comparison lens only. The 9-type guide lives in the Resistance Library (InfoWar ▸ Reading), with a disconfirming observation for each type.

cards.name: DiSC
cards.measures: Four work-style quadrants (Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, Conscientiousness). Psychologists question its predictive validity; peer-reviewed support is thin.
cards.misuse: Team-labeling and role assignment from a quadrant score.
cards.compatiblePractice: Useful only as vocabulary for describing stylistic differences you already observe in yourself across contexts.

cards.name: Dark Triad (behavior recognition)
cards.measures: Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy as trait measures in research. This app uses ONLY the behavior-recognition side: what exploitative patterns look like from outside.
cards.misuse: Labeling another person as a narcissist or psychopath from afar — which this app provides no tool for and will not build. Trait measures are for research, not for diagnosing people in your life.
cards.compatiblePractice: Name the tactic, not the person: 'guilt followed by urgency' is actionable; 'they are a manipulator' is a verdict that forecloses evidence. If patterns include threats or control, use the support card.
